summary: Describes the architecture for protocols and services supporting Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID and tracking, and related communications, meeting the requirements of RFC 9153.

eli5.summary: A plan for how drones announce who they are while flying and how others can check it.

questions: how does drone remote id work
subtitle: How drones can announce a verifiable identity in flight, using cryptographic IDs, DNS registries and existing Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Regulators require unmanned aircraft to be remotely identifiable, but the broadcast links used are tiny, so a trustworthy, hard-to-spoof identifier is difficult to fit in.
tldr.mechanism: DRIP uses Hierarchical Host Identity Tags (HHITs) as self-asserting IPv6-style identifiers, registers them in DNS-based public and private registries, and signs broadcast messages so that an Observer can build a chain of trust.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an architecture and entry point for the DRIP documents; it meets the requirements of RFC 9153 except GEN-7 QoS, which is left for future work.

today: RFC 9434 is an Informational RFC with no listed obsoleting or updating documents. It frames the DRIP work, and relies on RFC 9153 for requirements and RFC 9374 for the DET.

sections.title: Why Drones Need Remote ID
sections.content:
This RFC describes an architecture for protocols and services that support Unmanned Aircraft System Remote Identification and tracking (UAS RID), plus related communications. It follows the requirements in RFC 9153 and shows how all of them can be met, except GEN-7 QoS, which is left for future work.

Civil Aviation Authorities around the world are mandating UAS RID. They tend to cite industry consensus standards rather than specify techniques. The RFC builds on the ASTM standard F3411-22a, which defines one set of RID information and two ways to send it. DRIP aims to apply existing IETF standards and Internet infrastructure to fill the gaps.
sections.eli5: Many countries want drones to wear a name tag that others can read. This document is the big plan for making those name tags safe and checkable.

sections.title: Broadcast RID and Network RID
sections.content:
Broadcast RID is a direct, one-way broadcast from the unmanned aircraft over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, using MAC layer messages with no IP. It only covers aircraft within direct radio line of sight, with a range up to approximately 1 km. Internet access is only needed afterwards, to look up registry information using the received UAS ID.

Network RID works over the Internet. The UAS sends its data to a Network RID Service Provider (Net-RID SP), typically the UAS Service Supplier (USS) it flies under. A Net-RID Display Provider (Net-RID DP) answers an Observer's query about a 4-D airspace volume by collecting details from all Net-RID SPs with operations in that volume. The Discovery and Synchronization Service (DSS) helps USSs learn about each other's operations.

The ASTM standard prescribes the protocols between Net-RID SP, Net-RID DP and DSS. DRIP could standardize secure protocols between the UA and the ground control station, between the UAS and the Net-RID SP, and between the Net-RID DP and Observer devices.
sections.eli5: Broadcast is like a drone shouting its name to anyone nearby. Network is like the drone telling a central office, which tells anyone who asks about that patch of sky.

sections.title: HHITs as DRIP Entity Identifiers
sections.content:
The core idea is to use a Hierarchical Host Identity Tag (HHIT), defined in RFC 9374, as the DRIP Entity Tag (DET). A HHIT is a self-asserting IPv6-compatible identifier derived by hashing the entity's public key, called the Host Identity (HI). The HHIT embeds the registration hierarchy, which has 2 levels: a Registered Assigning Authority (RAA) and then a HHIT Domain Authority (HDA).

Broadcast RID imposes severe constraints. ASTM UAS ID type 4 (Specific Session ID) leaves 19 bytes after one byte of subtype index, and ASTM has allocated subtype 1 to IETF DRIP. Authentication type 5 leaves only 200 of the 201 bytes of an Authentication Message for DRIP. A self-endorsement of a HHIT can fit in as little as 88 bytes with Ed25519: the 16-byte HHIT, two 4-byte timestamps and the 64-byte signature.

Ed25519 is the mandatory-to-implement signing algorithm because it keeps the HI to 32 bytes. A UA equipped for Broadcast RID MUST be provisioned with its HHIT, the HI public key it came from, and the matching private key for signing. Registration with a DRIP Identity Management Entity (DIME) locks a HHIT to a specific HI, which defends against hash collisions and second-preimage attacks.
sections.eli5: The drone's name tag is made by scrambling its secret key into a short code. Because the code comes from the key, only the real drone can prove the tag is its own.

sections.title: Registration and Registries
sections.content:
DRIP registries hold public and private information about each UAS. The public registry gives trustable data such as endorsements of ID ownership and registration with the HDA. A DRIP identifier MUST be registered as an Internet domain name, so the DNS provides the public information: the HI through a HIP Resource Record, and pointers to the RAA and HDA. DNSSEC can protect information that is not inherently trustable, and the DNS entry can also signal revocation.

The private registry is similar to domain name registration data. When a DET is used as a UA's Session ID, the manufacturer-assigned serial number MUST be stored in a private registry that can be identified from the DET. If the flight is under UTM, the Operational Intent Identifier SHOULD be stored too. Registry operations (add, delete, update, query) can leverage the Extensible Provisioning Protocol and the Registry Data Access Protocol, and the registry must be findable from the UAS ID using the methods of RFC 9224. An access-controlled DNS or WebFinger are alternatives.
sections.eli5: There are two phone books. One is public and says whether a tag is real. The other is private and holds details like who owns the drone, shown only to people allowed to see it.

sections.title: Trust, Crowdsourcing and Contact
sections.content:
A self-asserting identifier is not enough. Broadcasting a DET, or sending data signed with its key, proves little because previously broadcast messages can be replayed. Only a DET plus a signature on novel, frequently changing and unpredictable data that the Observer can check, such as a signed Location/Vector message matching where the UA is actually seen, proves the sender holds the private key.

DRIP Authentication Messages combine two kinds of information: registration of the UA's ID in the claimed DIME, and sender signatures over both static and dynamic data. Together they let an Observer, online or offline, piece together a chain of trust. Observers that must work without Internet access MUST be provisioned with the public keys of the root registries or certificates for subordinate registries.

Broadcast RID has limited range, so the RFC proposes gateways that harvest broadcasts into UAS Traffic Management. Gateways could be pre-positioned or crowdsourced, since a smartphone with an app is enough. A CS-RID Finder is the gateway, and a CS-RID SDSP aggregates what Finders collect and can estimate UA locations by multilateration, independent of the self-reported locations. A message claiming a location far from the receiver can be flagged by a cheap consistency check.

DRIP Contact lets an Observer start a secure channel to the pilot, the USS or the aircraft itself, using the HI in the DET. Two preconditions apply: each party needs a way, typically DNS, to resolve the other's identifier to an IP address, and there must be bidirectional IP connectivity. One directly supported method is the HIP Base Exchange followed by a Bound End-to-End Tunnel.
sections.eli5: Showing a name tag is not enough, since it could be copied, so the drone also signs something fresh you can check. Phones nearby can pass along what they hear, and the tag helps you contact the pilot.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The HHIT hash is short enough to be vulnerable to a second-preimage attack. A receiver that only re-hashes the HI to check the HHIT could be fooled, so online receivers should verify the HHIT and HI with the HDA, and all receivers can use a chain of endorsements from a root of trust. Compromise of a DIME private key could do widespread harm, and specific key revocation procedures are still to be determined. The RFC says DRIP has not yet addressed post-quantum cryptography, and that denial of service by RF jamming cannot be prevented.

To resist replay, a receiver MUST NOT trust claims from an observed UA until it has a complete chain of endorsements and a message with nonce-like data signed by the DET's key.

For privacy, Broadcast RID can contain personal data such as the operator ID and the pilot location. DRIP's approach is symmetric encryption of that data using a session key known to the UAS and its USS. Authorized Observers get plaintext by asking a server to decrypt, or by getting the session key. If the UAS loses connectivity to its USS, the protection MUST NOT be used and the personal data is broadcast without protection.
sections.eli5: A fake tag could be made if someone worked hard enough, so listeners should double-check with the registry. Private details are locked in a box that only allowed people can open.
